To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
T cells from recipients of bone marrow grafts are defective in their ability to increase intracellular ionized Ca2+ concentration after binding the TCR-anti-CD 3 complex.
(1) the T cell receptor (TCR) is not functional after BMT; (2) this T cell defect may be due to a lack of expression of CD3; and (3) the T cell defect can be overcome by the administration of IL-2.

T cell receptor (TCR)-CD3 complex binding to monoclonal antibodies does not induce increases in intracelular ionized calcium concentrations in a substantial number of T lymphocytes from recipients after BMT.
In summary, our research is concerned with
immune dysfunction in recipients after bone marrow transplant (BMT).
the immune defects in T lymphocytes from recipients after bone-marrow transplantation (BMT) and the effects of these defects on the immune reconstitution of recipients after BMT.
the immunologic defects in T cells after BMT.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the defect is present in T cells from a majority of recipients after allogeneic or autologous BMT and that it persists in the T cells of some recipients for at least 1 yr.
the defect of T cell signal transduction in recipients of allogeneic or autologous BMT is not a failure of calcium flux after CD3-antibody binding.
the T cell signal transduction defect is not present in long-term recipients and is present in a substantial proportion of short-term recipients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the TCR signal transduction response is impaired in the majority of recipients early after allogeneic and autologous BMT, and this defect may be due to a defect in the TCR itself or to a defect in a downstream signal transduction event.
T cell function is defective early after BMT and that the defects are not restricted to a single T cell function.
there are multiple defects in T cell signal transduction after BMT.
The main takeaway from our work is that
T cell receptor-antigen receptor interactions can be used to study T cells from patients with immune dysfunction.
the TCR-antigen receptor signal transduction pathway is defective early after BMT and that the defect may be a contributing cause of the immune deficiency in these patients.
T cells in the early post-BMT period are not only functionally defective, but they also have a defect in signal transduction.
